chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Abu Ali al-Ash'ari from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar from Safwan from Jamil said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): The game, whether wild animals in his home or birds, does it become invalid for the pilgrim while he is in his house? He said, 'There is no harm in it; it does not harm him.'

The Sheikh (may God have mercy on him) said: If he kills a large number of locusts, then upon him is the blood of a sheep. And it is not permissible for the pilgrim to eat wild locusts, and it is permissible for him to eat sea locusts, except that he is obliged to pay compensation.

key_terms.دَمُ شَاةٍ: Blood of a sheep (a specific type of fidyah/compensation)
key_terms.يُحْرِمُ: He enters the state of consecration (Ihram)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a pilgrim killing locusts or keeping wild animals at home during Hajj?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies that mere possession of wild game does not break the state of iḥrām, distinguishing it from the act of killing. It further specifies that while consuming wild locusts is prohibited for the muḥrim, sea locusts are permissible provided the pilgrim pays fidyah, highlighting the nuanced distinction between different types of game in Shia jurisprudence. The text underscores the principle that accidental or specific types of hunting require compensation rather than invalidating the pilgrimage entirely.
